title: maintenance-lanes-and-upgrade-policy-matrix-for-runtime-api-sdk-console
creator: Aisha Kumaran
description:
Purpose: define a practical, cross-surface policy that maps maintenance lanes (the long-lived support channels) to explicit compatibility guarantees, rollout gates, and upgrade tooling for runtime, public API, client SDKs, and Redwood Console.

Background: multiple teams need a single source of truth for which versions we continue to support for bug/security fixes, which versions receive performance/security backports, and where breaking changes are allowed. Current ad-hoc practices create confusion for customers and make rolling upgrades risky (notably for Dedicated/Private deployments).

Proposal summary (high-level):
- Introduce named maintenance lanes: "Current" (default short-lived), "Stable" (12-month maintenance), "Extended" (24-month LTS), and "Nightly/Canary" (experimental).
- Define per-surface guarantees and policy rows: runtime, public API, SDKs (JS/Python/Go), Console. Each row specifies supported versions, compatibility commitments (backwards/forwards), permitted fix classes (security, critical bug, non-critical), and SLA for patches.
- Rollout gates: automated compatibility test suites (golden prompts, integration smoke tests), canary percentages, runtime performance regression checks, and staged default route migration.
- Upgrade tooling: a cross-surface "upgrade-assistant" CLI and Console workflow that: detects customer surface versions, simulates compatibility matrix outcomes, recommends migration steps and quantized risk (low/medium/high), and automates safe rollout (canary -> ramp -> full).

Key elements of the matrix (examples):
- Runtime: Stable lane = ABI-stable within the lane (no model/kernel ABI breaks), binary patches allowed; Extended lane = only security and correctness patches; any performance or new-kernel changes require opt-in and a compatibility shim.
- Public API: Stable lane = semantic compatibility for existing routes; minor additions allowed with feature flags; major breaking changes require 6-month deprecation notice plus automatic fallback route for older clients.
- SDKs: Stable lane = pinned API surface with deprecation markers; each SDK version will carry a lane tag and an automated migration guide generated from code-level diffs.
- Console: UI/ux changes considered non-breaking if they don't modify saved objects APIs; persisted dashboard schema changes gated by migration jobs with preview and rollback.

Operational SLAs and timelines example:
- Stable: security fix within 7 business days, critical-fix within 14 days, non-critical bug fixes best-effort within release cadence.
- Extended: security fix within 14 business days, critical fixes best-effort; no non-critical commits.

Decision drivers and trade-offs:
- Stronger guarantees reduce forward agility for runtime/infra teams but increase enterprise confidence for Dedicated/Private customers.
- More lanes (e.g. 3+ lanes) increase test/CI surface; automation (compat tests, upgrade-assistant) mitigates maintenance cost.

Next steps (tech work):
1) Draft formal matrix artifact (spreadsheet + machine-readable YAML) that enumerates lanes vs surfaces vs guarantee cells.
2) Implement lane tags in release artifacts and changelogs (CI changes).
3) Add lane-awareness to compatibility test harness (runtime e2e + API contract tests + SDK integration tests).
4) Build a minimal upgrade-assistant prototype in the repo (CLI + Console integration).

Acceptance criteria:
- A published matrix doc in Confluence that is approved by Runtime, API, SDK, and Console leads.
- CI ensures lane tags are attached to every release pipeline.
- A prototype upgrade-assistant that can analyze a customer's deployed set of versions and emit a recommended safe rollout playbook.

Links to artifacts and references:
- Confluence draft: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RELEASE/pages/maintenance-lanes-draft (placeholder)
- Epic: RED-EPIC-1672 (release-infra: maintenance lanes & upgrade tooling)
- PR prototype (upgrade-assistant): https://github.com/redwood-inference/release-tools/pull/312
- Golden prompt suite dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/compat/golden-prompts

Risks:
- Underestimating the QA cost for guaranteeing ABI stability on the runtime; mitigation = additional fuzz and kernel regression tests in CI.
- Customers might delay upgrades; mitigation = clearer deprecation notifications and assisted migration through Console.

Open questions:
- What is the minimum viable lane set we can operate on Day 1? (Proposal: Current + Stable + Extended + Canary)
- How do we bill/support Extended lane customers operationally? SLA/contract required.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Confluence matrix published and reviewed by leads (Runtime/API/SDK/Console). 2) CI change adds lane tag metadata to every release artifact. 3) Compatibility test harness runs lane-specific suites. 4) Upgrade-assistant MVP can produce a canary->ramp->full playbook for a sample Dedicated customer.
decisions: Adopt 3 named commercial lanes (Current/Stable/Extended) plus Canary for experimental work
Require lane metadata to be embedded in release artifacts (build manifest, changelog)
Security fixes must be supported across Stable and Extended lanes per SLA
